title: CRA Technical-File Compiler Built Into CI
one_liner: A GitHub/GitLab app that assembles the Cyber Resilience Act technical documentation, Annex I evidence and draft declaration of conformity from every release, so compliance is a build artifact rather than a consulting project.
customer: Product-security leads and CTOs at connected-device makers with 20-300 engineers (smart home, industrial IoT, e-bikes, wearables, network gear, EV chargers) selling into the EU. Not the GRC team.
problem: CRA reporting duties began 11 Sep 2026, full application is 11 Dec 2027, and fines reach EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover. Manufacturers must keep versioned technical documentation (risk assessment, design, vulnerability handling, test evidence, SBOM), for roughly ten years or the support period. GRC platforms produce policy evidence, SBOM tools produce component lists, and consultants charge tens of thousands per product line for a file that goes stale on the next release.
solution: The app reads the repo, CI logs, SBOM (SPDX/CycloneDX), threat-model files and test results, then maps them to the Annex I essential requirements and vulnerability-handling duties. It posts gaps as pull-request comments ('no secure-update mechanism documented'). Each release yields a signed, timestamped technical-file bundle (PDF plus machine-readable), a declaration-of-conformity draft, a support-period statement and a diff from the previous release.
why_now: Reporting is already live and full application is 15 months away, so products in design today are locking in the choices that determine compliance cost. Harmonised standards are still arriving, so teams need structured evidence now rather than a finished standard to tick off.
revenue_model: SaaS at $1,500-6,000/month per product line, EUR 5-15k onboarding, and referral revenue from test labs and notified bodies.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders assume Vanta/Drata-style GRC platforms will absorb the CRA. But the CRA is product regulation: the evidence lives in Git, CI and design docs and must be regenerated each release. That is a developer-tool, bottom-up sale to engineers, not a compliance-officer sale.
first_30_days: Interview 15 device makers via CRA meetups and open-source foundations working on CRA. Build a CLI that ingests a CycloneDX SBOM plus a small cra.yaml and emits a skeleton technical file. Run three paid pilots (EUR 3-5k) that produce each firm's first file, and publish the Annex I checklist as open source to draw inbound.

title: Ground-Truth Diligence for GPU-Backed Lenders
one_liner: Independent-engineer-style diligence and monthly monitoring on the part of a data center build that satellites cannot see: the last 90 days before ready-for-service.
customer: Private credit funds, banks and ABS investors lending against GPUs and neocloud contracts; insurers underwriting delay risk; AI labs and enterprises signing take-or-pay capacity who need to know if the promised RFS date is credible.
problem: GPU-backed loans and offtake contracts are priced on a ready-for-service date. Satellite vendors (SynMax and Industrial Info Resources now cover 2,600+ projects weekly) can show steel, cooling towers and generator yards, but they cannot see the failure zone: utility permission to energize, MV switchgear energization, Level 4/5 commissioning and IST results, liquid-cooling flush and pressure tests, fiber-plant acceptance, OEM startup-tech availability. Percent complete on pay applications is front-loaded and misleading. Meanwhile GPUs costing millions per rack sit idle and depreciate while interest accrues, and lenders are capping neocloud exposure. Traditional IEs are power-plant-oriented, slow and expensive.
solution: A 'Readiness Ladder' of about 40 binary, evidence-backed milestones (utility energization letter, gear serials and bills of lading, Cx level sign-offs, IST pass/fail counts, CDU flush logs, open-punch burn-down rate, OEM startup-tech calendar). Score each project and re-score monthly. Output a probability of RFS by date and covenant or draw-release triggers. Staff it with a bench of ex-data-center PMs and Cx leads who do desk review plus quick site visits. Sell as a 2-week second-opinion product first, then monthly monitoring, integrating vendor satellite feeds as an input rather than competing with them.
why_now: Neocloud credit risk is now the topic. Lenders are capping exposure, deals are stalling on credit risk, and GPU-debt structures (including vendor backstops) are proliferating. Analyses show roughly 40% of AI data center sites with possible delays and about half of 2026 capacity slipping, while operators publicly deny it. Satellite monitoring has commoditized the exterior, which makes the interior truth the scarce and valuable part.
revenue_model: $25K fixed-fee 2-week second opinions; $40K-120K full pre-close diligence; $8K-20K/month per facility monitoring; optional success-based fee for delay-risk insurance placement. Adjacent product: retained RFS-credibility scoring for AI labs choosing between capacity offers.
non_obvious_insight: Percent complete is the wrong metric. The last 5% of a data center can consume 25% of the calendar, and it is dominated by unbounded tasks: the commissioning punch-list burn-down rate and whether the OEM has a startup technician free that month predict RFS far better than construction progress. You can only read those signals if you have run an IST. Also, the RFS date on a marketing sheet is a sales number, not a schedule.
first_30_days: Recruit 6 retired or between-jobs Cx leads and PMs on 1099 contracts. Publish a free 'RFS credibility checklist' and a teardown of one publicly delayed project. Approach 5-10 private credit and infrastructure funds with data center or GPU-lending desks. Offer a fixed-fee $25K second opinion on one live deal, delivered in two weeks, and ask permission to reference the engagement anonymously.

title: Public-Records Vault for City Employee AI Chats
one_liner: Capture, retain, redact and produce every government employee's AI prompt and response as the public record it legally is.
customer: City clerks, county records officers and city attorneys at cities of 20-300K people that just rolled out AI assistants to staff.
problem: Every prompt and output from a government employee is likely a public record subject to retention schedules and open-records requests. Cities are turning AI on in Chattanooga-style rollouts with no retention system. A single request from a journalist could force manual digging through vendor logs the city may not control.
solution: Browser extension and API proxy that captures AI interactions across tools, tags them to retention schedules, redacts exempt content (personnel, law enforcement, attorney-client), and generates one-click productions for open-records requests. Litigation-hold support included.
why_now: Local AI adoption is now real, with police, school and bus-routing deployments. GenAI.mil users have built more than 100k agents. Records lawyers are starting to warn, and the first open-records fights over chatbot logs will land in 2026-27.
revenue_model: $8-40K per year per city by headcount, plus e-discovery production fees. Reseller channel via records-management vendors.
non_obvious_insight: AI adoption creates a records problem before it creates a safety problem. The clerk, not the CIO, has a legal deadline and a small budget line for exactly this.
first_30_days: Talk to 10 city clerks and 3 state records associations. Build the capture extension for two chat tools and a retention-schedule mapper. Pilot free with 2 cities that have announced AI programs, and convert on the first open-records request.

title: Managed Migrations When Models Get Retired
one_liner: We replay your agent's real traces on the replacement model, fix the regressions, and hand back a patched prompt and tool config with a pass/fail report before the deprecation date.
customer: Series A-C SaaS companies and enterprise automation teams running 1-20 production agents without a dedicated eval or ML team.
problem: Model versions are retired on schedules set by others (for example GitHub scheduled the removal of several Claude and Gemini versions in Copilot on 2026-09-01). When an agent is repointed to a newer model it keeps returning success codes while tool-call formatting, JSON adherence, refusal boundaries and token use silently change. Teams without eval infrastructure find out from customers.
solution: Fixed-fee migration sprints: capture golden traces, build assertions from tool traces, schemas and business rules, run baseline versus candidate models, tune prompts and tool descriptions, and report accuracy, latency and cost. A subscription Sunset Watch tracks about 20 providers' deprecation calendars and opens migration tickets automatically, with a self-serve replay tool later.
why_now: Retirement cadence accelerated across 2025-26, agents with multi-step tool use are more fragile than chat apps, and falling token prices tempt teams to switch models constantly.
revenue_model: $8-$25k per migration sprint and $1-3k/month for Sunset Watch.
non_obvious_insight: The customers who most need migration cannot afford an eval team, which is why Y2K, Java and Windows migrations became services businesses. Deprecation calendars are set by providers, so demand is scheduled and forecastable.
first_30_days: Publish a public deprecation calendar and migration-risk checklist. Cold-offer sprints to 30 companies visibly on soon-to-be-retired models (found via job posts and public integrations). Do 2 discounted pilots.

title: Restock Monitors Turned Competitor Sell-Through Radar
one_liner: Repurpose the Discord restock-monitor infrastructure teen resellers run into a SKU- and size-level sell-through index for DTC brands and the investors and acquirers who buy them.
customer: Founders and merchandisers of DTC brands who want to see rivals' sell-through ($199 to $799 per month), boutique retail buyers, and consumer-focused funds, search-fund buyers and e-commerce acquirers who need diligence on a Shopify brand ($2,000 to $5,000 per report).
problem: Everyone in e-commerce has to guess how fast a competitor's hero product actually sells. Public analytics tools give traffic estimates, not sell-through by size, color or restock. Buyers of small Shopify brands take the seller's word for 'we sell out in days' and get burned.
solution: Teen resellers already run monitors on thousands of storefronts: each one polls public product feeds so a Discord ping fires the instant a size restocks. The same stream, kept as history, shows how fast each variant flips to sold-out, restock cadence, drop timing, markdown timing, price changes and collection moves. Package it as a weekly Sold-Out Index and an on-demand brand report: 'their black M hoodie sold out in 41 minutes twice, restocked every 3 weeks, and they cut price 15% after the tariff news'. Use public storefront signals only, with no checkout tricks, and honor rate limits and terms.
why_now: Tariff-driven price changes in 2025-26 have every brand asking what rivals did to prices and when. DTC brand acquisition and roll-up activity means more diligence is being done on tiny Shopify brands. LLMs now classify messy product titles into a clean taxonomy cheaply, which was the hard part of turning monitor pings into an index.
revenue_model: Subscription for brand and retail buyers ($199 to $799 per month), one-off diligence reports ($2,000 to $5,000), and a data feed for funds later.
non_obvious_insight: The restock-alert economy is really an accidental, huge, always-on sensor network for the long tail of DTC commerce. Enterprise alt-data vendors ignore small brands because they think there is no data on them. Resellers have been logging exactly that data every minute for years. The unit of value is sold-out speed by variant, which reseller monitors track and analytics vendors do not.
first_30_days: Take the existing monitor feed for about 2,000 storefronts in streetwear, sneakers and collectibles and start logging history now, because history is the asset. Publish a free weekly Sold-Out Index thread on TikTok and X to get inbound. Sell 10 founders a $199 competitor watchlist by DM. Pitch one search-fund or acquirer community for a paid diligence report at $2,000 to check willingness to pay.

title: Genki Tap: Konbini Clerks as Paid Elder Watchers
one_liner: Pay convenience-store staff to log a three-second 'seen and how they seemed' note on enrolled elderly regulars, and alert family and local support centers when someone goes quiet or drifts.
customer: Adult children living outside Osaka with a widowed or single parent in the city, at about ¥1,480 a month. Later customers are municipal community support centers (chiiki hokatsu shien centers) paying per enrolled senior, and eventually banks, trust banks and insurers that need early cognitive-decline and fraud signals.
problem: In 2025, 76,941 people died alone at home in Japan, 58,919 of them aged 65 or older. The Cabinet Office estimates about 22,222 were found after 8 or more days. Municipalities have signed 'elder-watching network' MOUs with konbini, post offices and newspaper carriers, but they are unpaid goodwill. The clerk notices, if that clerk happens to be on shift and cares, and the observation never becomes structured data. Owners know who has not come in for three days. We notice the customer buying the same item twice in a day, paying slowly with coins, forgetting the wallet, or getting confused at self-checkout. None of it reaches the family or the ward.
solution: The senior gets a keychain NFC tag or simply says a name. At the register, staff tap a ¥1,500 reader or a tablet and press one of three buttons: fine, a bit off, worried. If an enrolled senior is not seen for 48-72 hours, the system messages the family and a designated neighbor, then the local support center. The family gets a weekly digest such as 'came Mon, Wed, Thu; usual purchases; once forgot wallet'. The store earns ¥300-500 per enrolled senior per month, so the attention is paid for and survives shift changes. Consent is opt-in, data is minimal, and the escalation path runs through licensed care managers.
why_now: The National Police Agency now publishes annual solitary-death counts, and the 2025 figures show no decline. Municipalities are legally responsible for loneliness and isolation measures under the 2024 loneliness law. Post-2024 summer heat deaths at home have raised demand from families. Cashless and prepaid-card fraud aimed at seniors is also rising, so a clerk who already knows the customer is the best front-line filter.
revenue_model: Family subscription of ¥1,480 a month, of which ¥300-500 goes to the store. Municipal or support-center contracts pay per enrolled senior. Later, anonymized cognitive-drift signals feed paid programs from banks, trust companies and insurers concerned about dementia-related frozen assets and fraud.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource in elder monitoring is not sensors or AI, it is a trusted human who sees the person daily and is already 24/7 in the neighborhood. Municipal networks fail because the clerk's attention is unpaid and unstructured. A ¥300 payment plus a three-button interface turns free goodwill into reliable, recurring, auditable data. The store that sees the drift first is the konbini, not the clinic.
first_30_days: Enroll 8-10 owners in Ikuno, Nishinari, Higashinari and Abeno wards, starting with my own three stores. Use a LINE OA for families and cheap NFC readers or a phone app for staff. Identify 30 regulars whose adult children live in Tokyo, Nagoya or Fukuoka and pitch them by phone; aim for 50 paying families at ¥1,480. Sign an MOU with one community support center as the escalation partner. Log every alert and outcome so the pilot produces evidence for a municipal contract.

title: Offline Distilled Agent Box for Denied Networks
one_liner: Ruggedized GPU box that runs small models distilled from a unit's own GenAI.mil agents, with zero connectivity.
customer: National Guard and reserve units, Army and Marine tactical staffs, border and disaster-response agencies, and defense integrators serving units in disconnected or denied environments.
problem: GenAI.mil is unclassified only and needs connectivity, yet users built more than 100k custom agents. The CDAO says compute is the binding constraint, and classified models cannot train in commercial data centers. Units in the field cannot use any of it.
solution: A service that takes a unit's approved agent workflows on GenAI.mil, distills them into small open-weight models with tool wrappers, and ships them on a rugged 1-2 GPU box with a one-screen interface. It updates by sneakernet with signed model bundles.
why_now: Open-weight small models are now good enough for narrow tasks. Right-sizing to cut inference cost is an explicit DoD priority, and model-vendor politics make owning a portable, vendor-independent model attractive.
revenue_model: $40-90K per box and $2-5K per month for update and distillation services. Government pilot funding via SBIR or CSO awards.
non_obvious_insight: The 100k user-built agents are an unwritten requirements document for what warfighters want. The winner distills the demand signal, not the model.
first_30_days: Ask 3 Guard units for one repetitive workflow (maintenance triage, reporting). Build a demo on commodity hardware with an open-weight model. Apply for one SBIR topic and ask an integrator for a paid subcontract.

title: Accessibility Disclosure Kit for US Independent Hotels
one_liner: A phone-based room-measurement kit that produces the accessibility details federal law requires on booking pages, before serial plaintiffs sue.
customer: US independent hotels and small groups of 30-300 rooms, franchisees, and the ADA-defence law firms who refer them.
problem: The federal hotel reservation rule (28 CFR 36.302(e)) requires booking systems to give enough detail about accessible rooms for guests to judge suitability, yet most sites just say 'ADA room'. Serial-filer suits repeat across the same properties and cost thousands each to settle. AI booking assistants also need structured answers on step-free showers and bed heights.
solution: A staff app guides a 20-minute walkthrough per room type using phone measurement and photos (door widths, turning space, shower type, bed height, grab bars). It generates compliant descriptions and a structured feed for OTAs, Google and AI assistants, then monitors listings for drift and provides a litigation-readiness pack.
why_now: Hotels are now being listed in AI assistants that demand structured attributes, and phones with depth sensing make measurement cheap. Serial-filer litigation continues, which gives the wedge and the budget.
revenue_model: USD 600-1,500 one-time per property plus USD 25-60 per month for monitoring, with rev-share to referring law firms.
non_obvious_insight: The lawsuit gets you the budget and the structured data is the moat. Detailed accessibility data is the missing input for agent booking, and accessible travel is an underserved segment.
first_30_days: Partner with 2 ADA-defence firms. Run a free scan showing what a serial filer sees on 100 hotel websites as lead-gen, and sell a USD 499 audit to 20 properties.

title: Supplier-Owned Origin Passport for Tier-2 Shops
one_liner: A portable, supplier-owned origin and metal-content passport that answers every customer's questionnaire once.
customer: Tier-2 and tier-3 suppliers with 10-200 employees in the US, Mexico and Canada. Buyers pay for portfolio dashboards.
problem: USMCA was not renewed on 2026-07-01 and now faces annual reviews through 2036. USTR flagged simplified compliance for smaller suppliers. CBP is prioritizing origin verification. Full-value duties depend on HTS class, metal weight and melt origin per SKU. Every buyer sends a different spreadsheet, and small suppliers re-answer them all with errors that expose buyers to penalties.
solution: Guided intake for BOM, mill certs (melt and pour country extracted from MTR PDFs), HTS and USMCA tariff-shift or regional-content calculation, kept as a versioned, signed record. The supplier shares subsets with each buyer by link. Buyers get standardized machine-readable packets and alerts when rules change. The first buyer is free, and suppliers pay to share with more.
why_now: Annual USMCA reviews create a permanent audit cycle, CBP is focused on origin verification, and Section 232 tiers now depend on melt origin. Regulators are asking for less burdensome small-supplier compliance.
revenue_model: $99-299 a month per supplier. $5-25k a year per buyer for dashboards and change alerts. Enterprise connectors later.
non_obvious_insight: Existing tools are sold to buyers and force suppliers into each buyer's portal. A supplier-owned credential flips the network effect, like a Plaid for origin. The USTR note on smaller suppliers signals regulators want a reusable format.
first_30_days: Target one cluster, such as 40 suppliers of one mid-size OEM in Monterrey/Laredo or Ohio. Get that OEM's buyer to say it will accept the passport. Build LLM extraction for mill certs. Onboard manually and aim for 10 paying suppliers.

title: AI-Run Cardiometabolic Care at ACCESS Prices
one_liner: An AI-first, pharmacist-supervised chronic-care program engineered to profit at Medicare ACCESS payment rates that break human-coach models.
customer: CMS pays it as an ACCESS participant ($360 per beneficiary per year initially, $180 follow-on, with half withheld pending outcomes). Medicare beneficiaries enroll at no cost. Later Medicare Advantage and Medicaid plans pay.
problem: ACCESS launched Jul 5, 2026 with ~150 participants. Payment works out to ~$30/month and Omada and Hinge sat out, so incumbents' cost structures don't fit. Primary care cannot titrate hypertension, lipid and prediabetes meds for millions of patients at this price.
solution: A mailed validated BP cuff and scale, voice-AI check-ins, protocolized titration of low-cost generics (ARB or CCB, statin, ezetimibe, metformin) and low-dose oral GLP-1 maintenance. Pharmacist and NP co-sign changes, with autonomous renewals only where state sandboxes allow (Utah's Jan 2026 AI renewal pilot covers 190 meds but excludes injectables and controlled substances).
why_now: ACCESS is live with rolling cohorts and a Jan 1, 2027 start. Oral GLP-1s are now first-line accessible, real-time voice AI is deployable, and a state has legally let AI renew chronic prescriptions.
revenue_model: CMS outcome-aligned payments of $360/year initial and $180/year follow-on per beneficiary. Target unit cost under ~$150/year for 50%+ margin, plus outcome-linked upside.
non_obvious_insight: At $30 per member per month the winner is whoever gets cost per member under about $12/month, which is an AI-to-pharmacist ratio problem, not a product problem. Big digital-health brands are structurally excluded.
first_30_days: Confirm the current CMS application window for the Jan 1, 2027 cohort. Meanwhile pilot 200 cash or MA patients with cheap cuff kits through a partner pharmacy, measure BP control and unit cost, and recruit a pharmacist supervisor and medical director.

title: Celebration-of-Life Concierge Using Restaurants' Dead Hours
one_liner: A flat-fee, turnkey memorial-gathering service for families who buy a cheap direct cremation and then have to improvise a goodbye, hosted in restaurants, breweries and hotel rooms during their empty weekday hours.
customer: Adult children (45-65) who bought direct cremation and must host 40-100 guests. Distribution partners are low-cost direct-cremation providers and hospice bereavement teams. Venues (restaurants, breweries, event rooms) pay a commission for filled dead hours.
problem: Funeral homes are hated for opaque upselling, so families flee to direct cremation at roughly $1,000-$3,000. That unbundles the ceremony: the gathering still happens 2-6 weeks later, but nobody provides it. Families scramble to find a venue, catering, a slideshow, an officiant and a livestream for remote relatives, while the cremation provider has no product for the moment that most shapes the family's memory of them.
solution: One booking that covers venue, per-head menu, host or officiant, memory-board and slideshow, RSVP and guest messaging, livestream and a printed program. The family pays a flat planning fee. The venue keeps the food and beverage revenue and pays a commission. Cremation providers and hospices embed a link in their after-care emails and take a referral fee or white-label it as their own add-on. A vetted list of local celebrants and photographers sits underneath.
why_now: The US cremation rate reached about 63.4% in 2025 and direct cremation is the fastest-growing disposition. NFDA reports that a majority of people have attended a funeral event at a non-traditional location, so the behavior has already shifted while the supply side is still a patchwork of ad hoc rentals. Restaurants and breweries are hunting for private-event revenue in weekday afternoons.
revenue_model: Family pays $750-$1,500 planning fee, plus add-ons (livestream, officiant, printed programs). Venue pays 12-15% of the food and beverage minimum (a 60-guest gathering at $55-$80 a head is $3-5k of spend). Referral fee of about $100 per booking to cremation providers and hospices.
non_obvious_insight: The funeral industry unbundled its own most emotional and highest-margin product. Disposition is now a commodity, but the ceremony did not disappear; it moved two to six weeks later, out of the funeral home, into a category no one owns, and it comes with a no-panic timeline, so the family is willing to plan and spend on it. The scarce resource is not a chapel, it is a trusted person who takes care of the whole afternoon.
first_30_days: Pick one high-cremation metro (Portland, Seattle, Las Vegas or Phoenix). Sign 8-10 venues with private rooms and per-head menus. Get two direct-cremation providers and two hospice bereavement coordinators to send a 'what happens next' link to families. Run the first gatherings by hand with a shared calendar, a phone line and a single landing page. The first paid bookings should come through partner referrals within weeks, and the service can stay fully concierge until 30-40 gatherings show what to automate.

title: Royalty Marketplace for Expert Agent Skills
one_liner: Retired and displaced specialists package their procedures, judgment rubrics and worked examples as machine-loadable skill packs that companies' agents pull on demand, with per-run metering and royalties to the author.
customer: Enterprises and SMBs deploying agents in regulated or technical workflows pay $200-2,000 a month per seat or per run. Authors are displaced experts who earn royalties.
problem: Agents are competent generalists that fail on domain procedures (customs classification, prior-authorisation appeals, tax-exchange steps). Hourly expert gigs pay once, so expertise is consumed without ongoing income, and enterprises can't find vetted, tested procedures.
solution: A curated marketplace of skill packs in the open Agent Skills format (instructions, scripts and tests), each with an eval suite and author credentials, metered per invocation through an MCP gateway. Quality is scored on held-out test performance and versions update as rules change. Wedge: tariff and customs-compliance packs written by retired customs brokers.
why_now: The Agent Skills format (Oct 2025) and MCP are becoming standard across agent tools, tariff volatility since 2025 has created urgent demand for trade-compliance expertise, and experienced professionals are being displaced.
revenue_model: 25-30% take on subscriptions and per-run fees, plus enterprise private-skill hosting.
non_obvious_insight: Hourly data labor turns experts into a consumable, while royalties make them asset owners. A metered gateway makes value attributable, and the moat is trusted eval suites rather than the marketplace itself.
first_30_days: Recruit 8 retired customs brokers or trade-compliance professionals. Build 5 tested skill packs and an eval harness. Sell to 10 importers already using agents at $300 a month and measure error reduction.

title: Vacant-House Concierge for Parents Moving Into Care
one_liner: One monthly plan that insures, inspects, maintains and eventually sells the house left empty when a parent moves to memory care or dies.
customer: Adult children and executors (45-65), often out of state, acting under POA or as executor. The channels are elder-law and estate attorneys, memory-care sales directors and senior move managers.
problem: When a parent moves into care, the house sits empty for 3-12 months. Homeowners policies typically restrict coverage after 30-60 days of vacancy, and pipes, taxes, utilities, break-ins and mail scams pile up. Probate cases rose about 32% from 2020 to 2024, and exhausted heirs are unprepared.
solution: A $199-449 monthly plan: vacancy-compliant insurance via an MGA partner, weekly inspections with water, temperature and entry sensors, autopay of utilities, taxes and HOA from an estate or POA account, seasonal maintenance, mail forwarding, sibling portal, documentation for the estate accounting, then cleanout, staging and a sell-when-ready referral.
why_now: The 80+ cohort is growing about 36.6% over the decade, senior housing is at 90% occupancy so moves happen in crises, and the $6T wealth transfer is underway. Heirs are far-flung Gen X executors who need a service, not a checklist.
revenue_model: Monthly subscription, insurance commissions, cleanout and staging fees, and a referral or flat fee on the eventual sale.
non_obvious_insight: Estate-settlement startups start at death, but the costly, uninsured window opens at the care move, years earlier. Anchoring on that moment gives access to the family before competitors and before the house loses value.
first_30_days: In one metro dense with senior housing, recruit 10 estate and elder-law attorneys and five move managers, secure a vacancy-insurance MGA quote, and sign the first 10 homes at an introductory rate.

title: Court-Accounting Software for Family Conservators and Executors
one_liner: Statement-to-court-form automation for family members who must file annual accountings for a parent under conservatorship or through probate.
customer: Lay conservators, guardians and executors (Gen X children), plus probate attorneys, CPAs and professional fiduciaries who handle 20-200 cases.
problem: Roughly a million-plus adults are under guardianship or conservatorship, and probate cases rose about 32% from 2020 to 2024. Appointed family members must file county- and state-specific accountings with receipts and categories. Errors mean surcharges or removal, and lawyers or accountants charge $500-2,500 a filing.
solution: Connect bank accounts or upload statements, categorize against the state's court forms, flag court-sensitive items (gifts, related-party payments, unusual withdrawals), produce the accounting and receipt binder, and calendar deadlines. Include optional attorney review. Launch in California and Texas, where forms and rules are standardized.
why_now: 80+ growth means more incapacity and more estates. Elder fraud losses ($7.7B in 2025) are pushing courts to scrutinize guardians, and LLMs now parse statements accurately enough for categorization.
revenue_model: $399 a year per case for lay fiduciaries, and $79-150 per case per month for professional fiduciaries and law firms.
non_obvious_insight: Legal tech serves lawyers and estate-planning creation; nobody serves the family member who is legally required to be an amateur accountant. Court deadlines make the pain acute and the willingness to pay high.
first_30_days: Start with California and Texas. Build SEO around 'conservatorship accounting help', partner with probate attorneys, and sell the first 20 cases at $399.

title: Pay-on-Close Homebuyer Readiness for Builders
one_liner: A builder-funded coaching and underwriting-repair program for the roughly half of showroom visitors who cannot yet qualify, paid per closing instead of through rate buydowns.
customer: Production and regional builders and their affiliated mortgage companies. The builder pays $2,000-$5,000 per attributable closing.
problem: Lennar says nearly 50% of visitors in many markets cannot immediately qualify for a mortgage, and it gives about 12% of price in incentives on a $372K average price, or roughly $45K per home. KB Home's cancellation rate is 18% of gross orders (up from 17%), and it makes 'minor adjustments' to keep buyers qualified. Builders spend heavily on lowering the monthly payment and almost nothing on fixing the reasons buyers fail underwriting.
solution: A 60-120 day cohort program runs alongside the builder's sales funnel for prospects who fail pre-qualification. It has four parts: (1) debt-to-income triage with a plan to pay down or restructure the few accounts that cause most failures, (2) lender-coordinated rapid rescoring, (3) co-borrower matching and down-payment-assistance navigation across state housing finance agencies, employer housing programs and gift rules, and (4) rent and utility payment reporting. Milestones are shared with the builder's lender through a dashboard. The vendor is paid only when a buyer the program touched closes on a home in the builder's community.
why_now: Mortgage rates are rising again (Paychex references a recent 25 bp Fed increase), and Lennar says rate-buydown costs are climbing. Resale inventory is at a decade high and is competing directly with new homes. KB Home's Executive Chairman says pricing is declining in more markets. The cheapest lever left is converting buyers who are near qualification.
revenue_model: $2,000-$5,000 success fee per closed home attributable to a program participant. Optional $300 per enrolled prospect for the coaching workload, credited against the success fee. Lender referral fees where permitted and disclosed.
non_obvious_insight: Incentive budgets buy payment relief, not qualification, and the qualification gap is large. Lennar's Stuart Miller says nearly 50% of visitors cannot immediately qualify, average incentives are about 12% of a $372K price, and buydown costs are rising with rates (https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/17/lennar-len-q3-2026-earnings-call-transcript/). KB Home reports an 18% cancellation rate, an 85% mortgage capture rate and 'minor adjustments' to keep buyers qualified, and buyers 'want to play the market and hope that rates come down' (https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/23/kb-home-kbh-q3-2026-earnings-call-transcript/). Credit-repair vendors have a poor reputation, and lenders have no incentive to coach a borrower for months. A builder paying per closing, the way it pays a broker, is a distribution model none of them have.
first_30_days: Approach 10 regional builders (100-1,000 homes a year) and their affiliated lenders, offering a free 60-day pilot in 1-2 communities. Pull the builder's list of leads that failed pre-qualification in the last 6 months, ask a partner loan officer to tag the failure reason, and run a manual outreach and coaching pass with two HUD-certified housing counselors. Track conversions weekly and sign a success-fee agreement once 3 closings are attributable.

title: Book the Unbookable: Agents for Offline Suppliers
one_liner: A voice-and-WhatsApp agent phones, negotiates and confirms bookings with small inns, guides and boat operators that have no API, then turns each one into bookable inventory.
customer: Independent travel advisors and small DMCs first, later AI trip-planning apps and OTAs seeking long-tail inventory.
problem: The best small inns, agriturismi, ryokan, guides and boat operators take bookings by phone, WhatsApp or email in local languages, with deposits by bank transfer. Advisors spend hours per booking, AI agents cannot book them and OTAs do not list them. Hotel-side voice AI is crowded (for example Dextr AI's seed), but buyer-side is empty.
solution: A real-time multilingual voice and text agent calls or messages the supplier, checks availability, negotiates a net rate within the advisor's limits and sends the deposit. A human verifies the money step. Every completed booking builds a structured supplier profile (hours, languages, deposit rules) that becomes API-bookable next time.
why_now: Real-time voice models now handle 30+ languages, WhatsApp Business is universal, and agentic payment tooling exists. Shrinking booking lead times and rerouted travel create demand for fast alternatives beyond OTA inventory.
revenue_model: USD 20-60 or 3-5% of booking value per booking from advisors, SaaS for DMCs, and later a take rate from suppliers and inventory data licensing.
non_obvious_insight: Long-tail supply is invisible to agents because it lacks an API, not because it lacks quality. The cheapest API is a phone call made by a machine with a human closing the money step, and each call builds an inventory graph nobody owns.
first_30_days: Pick Japan, Italy and Greece. Recruit 15 independent travel advisors and process 100 bookings semi-manually with human voice operators shadowing the agent at USD 30 per booking. Measure time saved and conversion.

title: Evacuation Lift Registry Ending Double-Booked Buses
one_liner: A neutral county-level registry that guarantees each ambulance, wheelchair van and bus seat is promised to only one nursing home per storm, paid for by facilities and by carriers who finally get standby retainers.
customer: Paying: multi-site nursing home and assisted-living operators (SaaS per facility) and ambulance/NEMT/charter-bus operators (platform fee on standby retainers). Sponsoring: county emergency managers and healthcare coalitions using preparedness grants.
problem: The CMS emergency preparedness rule makes every facility hold transportation agreements, but no one checks whether the same 40 wheelchair vans and ambulances are 'contracted' by 300 facilities. GAO and post-Katrina research found carriers holding contracts with many facilities in one community, which works for a single-building evacuation and collapses when a whole county goes at once. Facilities learn at H-48 that their contract is one of a dozen identical promises. Carriers do not honor a promise they were never paid to hold.
solution: Borrow the military's lift-allocation discipline, where an asset can appear on the movement plan only once. Facilities reserve capacity by resident mix (ambulatory, wheelchair, stretcher, oxygen or vent-dependent), not by 'beds'. The registry totals promised demand against real vehicle capacity by county and flags oversubscription weeks before the season, then matches the gap to out-of-region carriers on paid standby. At activation it issues a departure-window movement table so convoys do not collide, plus manifest and accountability packets for each facility. Before activation it stores only aggregate counts by acuity, not PHI, which keeps HIPAA scope small.
why_now: The President's FEMA Review Council final report (May 7, 2026) recommends disaster response be 'locally executed, state managed, federally supported'. Counties and healthcare coalitions are inheriting logistics they never staffed, with less federal backfill. It is peak hurricane season, and post-acute care closures and consolidation are concentrating residents into fewer, larger buildings.
revenue_model: $150-400 per facility per month. Carriers pay 8-12% on standby retainers the platform brokers, which they never received before. Optional county or coalition license of $25-100k a year, funded by ASPR HPP or EMPG grants. Later, add-ons for dialysis centers, group homes and inpatient rehab.
non_obvious_insight: Vehicles are not the shortage. Unique promises are. Every evacuation failure post-mortem says 'not enough buses', but the fleet often exists and is simply committed many times over. Military movement planners never let one lift asset appear twice on a time-phased deployment plan, while civilian planners have nobody whose job is to check. Loading time is also the hidden constraint: a stretcher resident takes about 20 minutes to load, so acuity mix, not headcount, determines how many vehicles you need.
first_30_days: Pick one storm-prone county cluster (Tampa Bay, coastal Carolinas or Louisiana parishes). Ask 10 facilities to share their transport MOUs, which they must keep on file for CMS surveys anyway. Build the overlap heat map by hand in a spreadsheet, for example 'nine of your ten facilities are promised the same carrier'. Take it to the county emergency manager and the healthcare coalition coordinator. Convert 3-5 facilities to a paid pilot at about $200 a month and sign 2 carriers to retainer contracts. Build the product as Airtable plus a simple web form before writing real software.

title: Amps Not Acres: Power Headroom for Retrofits
one_liner: Headroom reports and a load-sequencing kit that let plants add machines inside existing walls without a new transformer.
customer: Owners and plant managers of 20-300 employee manufacturers, and machine-tool, compressor and robot dealers who need to know whether a customer can power what they sell.
problem: Site selectors and economic developers think reshoring is limited by land, buildings and permits. The data say otherwise. Factory construction is down 22-32% from peak, yet nondefense capital-goods orders hit a record $85.9B in July, so equipment is going into old buildings. Transformer and switchgear prices are up 89-96% since 2019 as data centers compete for the same gear. Utility service upgrades cost six figures and take a year or more.
solution: Step 1 is a Headroom Report. It pulls 12 months of utility interval data (Green Button) and uses measured demand (NEC 220.87 allows this) to show how many kW can be added, ready for a PE stamp. Step 2 is a clamp-on CT and PLC/gateway kit that staggers compressors, furnaces, welders and spindle start-ups to cap demand peaks. Step 3 adds an optional battery or thermal-storage partner for the residual gap.
why_now: Record capital-goods orders with $953B unfilled, prices for electrical gear up sharply, and reshoring that is happening in existing buildings. No incumbent sells 'create amps in software' to a 50-person shop.
revenue_model: $1.5-3k per report (dealers pay to close sales). $5-15k for hardware and install. $200-400 a month for monitoring. Referral fees from dealers and battery vendors.
non_obvious_insight: Nameplate capacity is not the constraint. Measured coincident peak is, and it is usually far below service rating. The scarce input is amps, and amps can be created by sequencing loads.
first_30_days: Pitch 10 machine dealers on the report as a free pre-sale add-on. Get interval data from 5 plants. Partner with a licensed PE for stamping. Assemble the first controller from off-the-shelf CTs and a PLC.

title: Sewershed Chemical Fingerprinting to Trace PFAS Sources
one_liner: A network of automated samplers plus non-target mass-spectrometry that bisects a city's sewer tree to find which industrial sources are putting PFAS into the plant.
customer: Wastewater utilities with biosolids or effluent PFAS problems, industrial pretreatment coordinators, state PFAS programs (Michigan's industrial pretreatment PFAS initiative is a precedent, from my background knowledge), and industrial dischargers that want an independent baseline. The utility or state pays.
problem: Wastewater plants cannot remove PFAS, yet they receive it from platers, landfills, textile, paper and semiconductor users, and they inherit the biosolids and effluent liability. Utilities treat sources as unknowable, so they cannot enforce or recover cost. Europe's polluter-pays wastewater rules will also need load attribution.
solution: Install 10-30 autosamplers per sewershed (pump stations and manholes). Analyze weekly composites through a partner lab using high-resolution mass spectrometry, total organofluorine and precursor assays. Use ML on the network tree to attribute loads to upstream sub-catchments, then deliver a source map and enforcement-grade evidence. First product: a 12-week campaign.
why_now: The 2027 monitoring wave, biosolids scrutiny, and falling costs of high-resolution mass spectrometry plus the COVID-era playbook for sewer-network sampling all converge.
revenue_model: $120-300k per campaign, $60-150k/yr surveillance subscriptions, and cost-recovery success fees.
non_obvious_insight: A sewer network is a tree, so 15 samplers can bisect to a source in weeks, like contact tracing. The buyer is the utility's legal and finance side seeking cost recovery from polluters, not the environmental regulator.
first_30_days: Sign one small city or regional plant with a known biosolids problem, or a state program. Partner with a commercial lab that has non-target capability instead of buying instruments. Run a pilot at eight nodes and produce a source-bisection map.

title: Sundowning Night Companion Speaking in Family's Voice
one_liner: A bedside device that detects night waking and reorients a person with dementia in a voice they consented to, escalating to a caregiver or remote night aide.
customer: Family caregivers of people with moderate dementia at home (about 15% provide 60+ hours a week), memory-care communities with thin night ratios, and home-care agencies with overnight cases.
problem: Night waking is a top reason families place a loved one. Overnight aides cost $300-450 a night, and families otherwise absorb 3 am crises. Generic AI companions are seen as deceptive or are not built for dementia.
solution: A bedside speaker or tablet with radar or audio wake detection plays short, clinically scripted reorientation lines in a familiar voice (for example a spouse or child), seeded by a 'voice will' the person records and approves while they still have capacity. It escalates to the caregiver's phone with two-way voice, then to a paid remote night aide, and logs sleep patterns for the neurologist. Guardrails: no impersonation of the deceased, and clinician sign-off.
why_now: Voice cloning from seconds of audio and on-device speech models are cheap in 2026. NY, FL and NJ are giving away ElliQ, showing public payers buy companionship tech, and 23% of 65+ now use ChatGPT, so acceptance is rising.
revenue_model: $199 hardware plus $39-59 a month for families, $30-50 per bed per month for memory care, and remote night-aide add-on fees.
non_obvious_insight: Ethics is the product: an advance 'voice will' turns a controversial deception into a consented comfort, like an advance directive for how you want to be soothed. Night is the least automated and most expensive shift.
first_30_days: Build on a commodity smart speaker with scripted lines, recruit 10 families through Alzheimer's support groups and one neurologist, and measure night-waking events over four weeks. Convene a geriatric psychiatrist and an ethicist as advisors.

title: Payroll-Deducted Paylater Refinance for Factory Workers
one_liner: Consolidate minimum-wage workers' paylater and online loans into one payroll-deducted instalment, sold to the employer as retention.
customer: Indonesian manufacturers and retailers with 1,000+ minimum-wage staff, especially in Java's industrial belts; employers pay a fee and a partner lender funds.
problem: Paylater financing reached Rp43.28T in May and online lending Rp100.69T, and defaults are rising among minimum-wage workers. Collection harassment causes absenteeism and turnover.
solution: Consolidate a worker's paylater and pinjol debts into one lower-rate loan repaid via payroll, funded by a licensed multifinance or bank partner. The wedge is three factories in Bekasi and Karawang.
why_now: OJK scrutiny is rising and the 2026 macro squeeze is pushing defaults up.
revenue_model: 1-2% origination plus lender spread share, and an employer fee of Rp10-15k per worker per month.
non_obvious_insight: The paylater trap is an HR problem before it is a credit problem, and the employer is the only party with payroll access and a reason to care.
first_30_days: Interview HR heads at three factories and pilot with 200 workers using a partner lender.

title: Contingency Recovery of Unpaid Implant Carve-Outs
one_liner: Find and collect the implant and device carve-out payments that hospitals and surgery centers are owed but never bill, because the invoice lives in accounts payable and not in the billing office.
customer: Physician-owned spine and orthopedic ASCs, plus small and mid-size hospital ortho/spine/cardiac service lines, with commercial payer contracts that carve out implants. Paid 20-30% of recovered dollars.
problem: Many commercial contracts pay implants and high-cost devices separately, at invoice cost plus a markup, but only if the vendor invoice is submitted with the claim. The implant log is in the OR record, the invoice is in supply chain or AP, and the claim is built by billing. Nobody connects them. The claim goes out with L8699 or revenue code 027x lines at billed charges, and the payer pays $0 for the device or folds it into the case rate. The payment posts as 'paid', so nobody notices the loss. This is $5k-$50k per case for spine and joint work.
solution: Ingest the implant log (manufacturer, catalog and lot numbers), AP invoice PDFs (parsed with an LLM), contract carve-out terms extracted from the PDFs, and the 837/835 files. Compute expected carve-out payment versus actual, auto-assemble invoice attachments per payer rules, and file corrected claims and appeals inside timely-filing windows. Run it as a service for the first clients (manual, coder-led), then automate the matching.
why_now: CMS's CY2026 outpatient rule began phasing out the inpatient-only list and added many procedures, mostly musculoskeletal, to the ASC-covered list. More device-heavy spine and ortho cases are moving to ASCs whose small billing staffs have never dealt with carve-outs. Payers are also using AI-driven payment integrity that makes missing attachments an automatic zero.
revenue_model: 20-30% contingency on recovered carve-out payments. After the first recovery, convert to $1.5-4k/month prospective monitoring per facility.
non_obvious_insight: The loss is invisible in every standard revenue-cycle KPI. Denial rate looks fine and AR looks fine because the line paid 'as billed under the case rate'. The only way to see it is to lay the supply chain invoice next to the contract term next to the 835. Billers know it happens. Supply chain does not know payers pay for it. Finance never audits it. That gap between three departments is the earned secret.
first_30_days: Pick 10 physician-owned spine and ortho ASCs through ASCA chapters and surgeon-owner LinkedIn outreach. Offer a free 90-day lookback audit, since contingency means zero risk to them. Each needs to share 835s, implant logs, invoices and the top three commercial contracts. Do the first three audits by hand with a coder and a spreadsheet, and use the dollars found as the sales collateral. Then automate the invoice parsing.

title: Phantom Load Vetting Desk for Rural Utilities
one_liner: A fee-based 'is this data center developer real?' diligence service for electric co-ops and municipal utilities drowning in 100-1,000 MW inquiries from shell LLCs.
customer: G&T and distribution electric cooperatives, municipal utilities and PUDs (5-person engineering staffs, no data center experience). Secondary: state economic development offices and county governments granting abatements. The utility or its G&T pays per inquiry or on retainer.
problem: Every small utility with transmission access is now getting inquiries for 200-1,000 MW campuses from LLCs formed 90 days ago. Each one eats study money, planning time and political capital, and a wrong bet strands ratepayer-funded infrastructure. Texas's proposed SB 6 rule (16 TAC 25.194, final rule due by end of 2026) would require $50,000/MW of financial security before a study and disclosure of duplicate requests. That pushes speculators into neighboring states and co-ops with softer tariffs. Small utilities have no way to tell a real project from a PowerPoint.
solution: A standardized 12-point 'physical reality' test built from paper trails that real projects leave and phantom ones cannot. (1) Air permit applications for generators, where the genset count implies the MW. (2) An OEM order acknowledgment or slot reservation for MV transformers and switchgear, plus a delivery date that fits the claimed energization date. (3) Recorded site control (deed or option). (4) Water and stormwater filings. (5) A named tenant LOI or offtaker. (6) A GC or EPC that has actually built a campus. (7) A financing letter. (8) Tax-abatement filings. (9) LLC principals cross-checked against other states' filings, to catch the same MW shopped to five utilities. (10) A power-density and cooling design consistent with the load ask. (11) Local land-use posture. (12) Team track record. The deliverable is a red/amber/green memo, a recommended security amount, and a milestone-gated study structure the utility can put in its ESA. Add-ons are a large-load tariff and ESA term-sheet template and a duplicate-request registry that co-ops in a region can pool.
why_now: Large-load tariffs and collateral rules are landing right now: Texas SB 6 (signed June 2025, PUCT rule proposed March 2026, final expected by 12/31/2026), plus AEP Ohio-style minimum-demand tariffs. Each new collateral regime displaces phantom load to the next-weakest utility. Transformer lead times of 3-5 years and switchgear sold out into 2028 mean that a real project without an equipment slot is not real, which gives a very cheap and reliable test. About half of announced 2026 builds are delayed or canceled, so utilities are burned and skeptical.
revenue_model: $7.5K-25K per inquiry vetting memo; $60K-150K/yr retainers for G&T co-ops that field 10+ inquiries a year; $25K-50K one-time tariff/ESA template packages; later a subscription to a multi-utility duplicate-request registry. Utilities can often pass the cost to the applicant as a study-deposit line item.
non_obvious_insight: Outsiders think the hard part of large-load planning is forecasting demand. Insiders know real projects are betrayed by equipment, not slides. A serious 300 MW developer has a transformer slot, a generator count on an air permit and a GC on payroll before the utility ever hears the name. A phantom has none of those. The tell is the logistics trail, and nobody at a 5-person co-op knows where to look. Texas's high collateral will also export the phantom problem to everyone else.
first_30_days: Build scrapers for state air-permit databases in 6-8 states and county deed/LLC records for 3 co-op service territories. Ask 3 co-op contacts (via state electric cooperative associations or a G&T's planning group) for their last 10 inquiries and run free back-tests on how they turned out. Publish a one-page '12 signs your data center inquiry is real' on LinkedIn and co-op association channels. Convert the first 2-3 into paid $7.5K memos on live inquiries and ask for a G&T retainer.

title: Hardware-Origin Audits for Drones and Robots
one_liner: Teardown-level bill-of-materials and firmware audits that prove what is really inside a 'US-made' drone or robot, sold to small makers, to the public-safety and utility buyers who must prove compliance, and to insurers.
customer: US drone and robot makers with 5-100 employees selling to public safety, utilities, agriculture and federally funded programs. Buyers: county, city and state procurement offices and grant recipients. Insurers and lenders who need 'no covered components' assurance.
problem: The FCC barred new DJI and Autel models in Dec 2025, US drone tariffs took effect in Sep 2026 with component tariffs in 2027, and China's export controls cover motors, batteries, radios and sensors. Buyers must show they bought compliant gear, but suppliers self-declare, rebrand and reroute. Procurement staff cannot inspect a flight controller. After the IEEPA tariff-refund saga, customs origin claims will draw scrutiny. Unitree G1 at about $16k tempts robot buyers into the same problem.
solution: An auditor plus registry. Teardown-level BOM verification (identify chips and modules, firmware and network-callback tests for covered-vendor endpoints, cross-check of supplier declarations and customs documents). It produces a signed origin and compliance dossier per model and lot. A public registry lets procurement staff query a model against state and federal restrictions.
why_now: The FCC action, tariffs and Chinese export controls all landed between Dec 2025 and Sep 2026. Domestic supply is emerging (Amprius won a $75M award for 500 Wh/kg cells), and dozens of new entrants all claim 'American-made'. A number of state laws also restrict agencies from buying Chinese drones (specifics to verify).
revenue_model: $8k-$30k per product audit for makers. $1k-$3k per re-certification on a BOM change. $2k-$5k/yr buyer-side registry subscription for agencies. Lot-level spot-check fees. Referral fees from insurers.
non_obvious_insight: When a ban creates a market, the scarce asset is belief in compliance, not the compliant product. The audit fee is a tax on every new entrant, and buyers fear being embarrassed by an audit finding. Inputs are cheap (a bench, a spectrum analyzer, firmware tooling) and one engineer can produce the first audits. The same dossier doubles as customs-origin evidence.
first_30_days: With maker consent (or from public teardowns), audit 5 currently marketed 'American-made' drones and publish the methodology. Offer three small US makers a $5k pre-audit with a money-back guarantee. Sell 3 full audits at $10k-$15k. Pitch a state public-safety procurement association on the registry.

title: Blue Tarp Index: Adjuster Ground Truth for ILS
one_liner: A subscription that sells cat-bond and reinsurance investors what veteran field adjusters can see in the first 10 days after a disaster, before any model or carrier report exists.
customer: ILS funds, cat bond trading desks, reinsurance-broker analytics teams, and hedge-fund or equity analysts covering Florida, Gulf and California-exposed carriers. Roughly $30k-$120k per year per team.
problem: Post-event loss estimates swing wildly (Milton was pegged anywhere from a few tens of billions up, and cat-bond implied-loss marks moved daily) and settle slowly. The cat bond market is now about $65.6B outstanding after a record $17.6B of H1 2026 issuance, and most of that capital marks to modeler guesses and carrier press releases. Investors have no structured ground truth for the variables that decide severity: how many roofs really failed, whether demand surge is 10% or 40%, and whether contractors can staff repairs at all.
solution: A vetted panel of 60-150 independent veteran cat adjusters files 10-minute standardized mobile observations on publicly visible conditions only: blue-tarp density per 100 roofs on sampled blocks, roofing debris and dumpster counts, mystery-shopped contractor and tarp-crew quotes ($/sq, lead times), hotel and RV occupancy, and adjuster deployment density. Outputs are an event dashboard, a 'Blue Tarp Index' and a demand-surge index within 72 hours to 10 days, a weekly note, and paid expert calls. Hard rule, reviewed by counsel: no claim-file, policyholder or carrier-confidential information, only public observation and market pricing, aggregated and anonymized.
why_now: Cat bond and ILS capital hit records in 2026, with over $120B of ILS capacity, so more money is exposed to event-loss uncertainty than ever. Claims-adjuster employment fell about 21% year over year through May 2026 as carriers automate, which leaves a large pool of experienced people who need income and are cheap to recruit. The very quiet 2026 Atlantic season (no hurricane until at least Sept 11) gives a scrappy team time to build and back-test before the next event. Wildfire, hail and flood events also count as live tests.
revenue_model: Annual subscription tiers ($25k signal-only, $60k with expert calls, $120k+ bespoke event coverage), per-event pay-per-call expert sessions, and paid retrospective studies. Adjusters get $75-$150 per completed field report plus a revenue share pool. Gross margin is high because the data is field labor, not infrastructure.
non_obvious_insight: Models price wind and exposure, but severity in the real world is set by contractor capacity: how many roofers, tarp crews and drying crews physically exist within 200 miles. An adjuster feels that constraint on day 4 because they cannot get a tarp crew to a house, and nobody in finance measures it. Tarps are also what the policy pays for first, so their density is a fast, visible proxy for claim frequency. The hypothesis is testable by back-testing against Helene, Milton and the LA fires.
first_30_days: Recruit 25 laid-off or semi-retired cat adjusters from cat-adjuster Facebook groups, adjuster forums and LinkedIn. Draft the observation protocol and a counsel-approved compliance memo. Run a retrospective 'what we would have told you on day 7' study on Helene/Milton and the Jan 2025 LA fires using panel memory, public imagery and contractor pricing archives. Publish a free sample note, send it to 15 ILS portfolio managers and 5 broker analytics heads, and aim for 2-3 paid pilots ($15-25k) that include the retro study as a deliverable, with the first live test on spring 2027 hail or a wildfire.
